main.title: Ape Escape 3
main.subtitle: Ape-catching on television sets
main.summary: Ape Escape 3 is a 2005 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. It is part of the Ape Escape series.

cards.heading: Ape-catching on television sets
cards.text: Ape Escape 3 is a 2005 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. It is part of the Ape Escape series.

cards.heading: Morphs change how the heroes play
cards.text: Playing as either Satoru (Kei) or Sayaka (Yumi), gameplay follows that of the previous games in which the player must catch several monkeys by using various gadgets controlled with the right analogue stick. While there are fewer gadgets in this game than previous entries, a new feature in this game is the ability to morph into different forms through a device built by Aki. Some monkeys may also try to steal the player's Stun Club or Time Net and use it against them, and can even force them out of the level by catching them with their own net. Playing as Sayaka has an additional benefit; owing to her pop idol status, certain monkeys will go star-struck upon sight of Sayaka, allowing for an easy capture.

cards.heading: Mesal Gear Solid: Snake Escape
cards.text: A minigame featured in the game is Mesal Gear Solid: Snake Escape, a spoof of Metal Gear Solid (the name is a pun on "metal" (metaru) and "monkey" (saru)). In this game, players control Pipo Snake, a monkey loaded with Solid Snake's battle data, sent on a mission to rescue Snake and destroy a monkey-like Metal Gear. Gameplay is similar to Metal Gear Solid in which players have to use stealth and weapons to sneak around undetected and rescue prisoners. Players are equipped with a Banana Pistol for stunning enemies and Pineapple Grenades for breaking open flimsy walls. Similarly, the original PlayStation 2 editions of Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater include a Snake vs. Monkey mode in which Snake has to capture monkeys.

main.title: Fatal Frame III: The Tormented
main.subtitle: Grief opens a door during sleep
main.summary: Fatal Frame III: The Tormented is Tecmo's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 28 July 2005. Rei Kurosawa, Miku Hinasaki and Kei Amakura are drawn towards the Manor of Sleep after losing people close to them. Their connected experiences place a haunted dream beside the apparently safer spaces of ordinary life. The Camera Obscura returns as the means of confronting hostile spirits, making the player look directly at what is approaching. The third game builds its fear around the possibility that returning home or waking up may not fully end the encounter.

cards.heading: Grief opens a door during sleep
cards.text: Fatal Frame III: The Tormented is Tecmo's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 28 July 2005. Rei Kurosawa, Miku Hinasaki and Kei Amakura are drawn towards the Manor of Sleep after losing people close to them. Their connected experiences place a haunted dream beside the apparently safer spaces of ordinary life. The Camera Obscura returns as the means of confronting hostile spirits, making the player look directly at what is approaching. The third game builds its fear around the possibility that returning home or waking up may not fully end the encounter.

cards.heading: The photograph requires a closer look
cards.text: Exploration uses fixed third-person views, while raising the Camera Obscura shifts attention into a first-person frame. The player must judge when a spirit is close enough for an effective photograph without waiting until it can strike. Different protagonists bring different strengths and limitations into the manor, changing how a familiar danger can be approached. The camera makes defence inseparable from observation. Looking away may feel safer, but the useful action requires holding the threat within the frame and committing to the shot at a moment when its presence is increasingly difficult to ignore.

cards.heading: Make the familiar place less reliable
cards.text: Makoto Shibata returned as director and Keisuke Kikuchi as producer, with Ayako Toyoda composing and Tsuki Amano supplying the theme song. Shibata's nightmares helped shape the emphasis on horror emerging from familiar surroundings. The game was planned as the series' final PlayStation 2 entry and reached North America in 2005 and Europe in 2006, where it was called Project Zero 3. Reviews praised its atmosphere and story. Its central relationship between mourning, dreams and the home gives the recurring camera mechanic another emotional context, making the danger persist beyond the mansion's immediate walls.

main.title: Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan
main.subtitle: A cheer squad answers the call
main.summary: Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan is iNiS's Nintendo DS rhythm game about a cheer squad helping people overcome their troubles. A desperate cry summons the uniformed performers, and a Japanese pop song becomes the accompaniment to somebody's personal crisis. The player directs the encouragement with a stylus while a comic-strip story unfolds above. Each short episode gives the same musical actions another purpose. Precision is still measured as a score, but a successful performance is also a way of getting a character through an improbable difficulty.

cards.heading: A cheer squad answers the call
cards.text: Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan is iNiS's Nintendo DS rhythm game about a cheer squad helping people overcome their troubles. A desperate cry summons the uniformed performers, and a Japanese pop song becomes the accompaniment to somebody's personal crisis. The player directs the encouragement with a stylus while a comic-strip story unfolds above. Each short episode gives the same musical actions another purpose. Precision is still measured as a score, but a successful performance is also a way of getting a character through an improbable difficulty.

cards.heading: Keep the fighting spirit alive
cards.text: Targets on the touchscreen ask for timed taps, traced phrases and repeated spinning movements. A closing ring identifies the moment to strike, while more precise inputs award more points and restore more of the constantly draining spirit meter. Missing a beat lowers it further. The controls are simple to describe, but maintaining a sequence demands listening and concentration. Flames grow behind the squad as a combo builds, making a sustained run visible as well as audible. The cheering becomes more intense because the player is keeping it together.

cards.heading: The story listens to the player
cards.text: At intervals the musical action pauses for a scene showing how the person being helped is progressing. A strong spirit meter produces an encouraging outcome; a weak one brings another setback. Those changes give the song's sections a dramatic rhythm of their own. Replaying can improve both the score and the confidence with which the scene unfolds. Ouendan finds a lively connection between an abstract timing challenge and ordinary human determination, using exaggerated situations to make the act of helping somebody feel immediate and funny.

main.title: Shadow Hearts: From the New World
main.subtitle: A new cast crosses an unfamiliar America
main.summary: Shadow Hearts: From the New World is Nautilus's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 28 July 2005. Johnny Garland, an amnesiac private investigator, travels with Shania in pursuit of the dangerous Lady through an alternate Prohibition-era America. The setting combines recognisable places and history with supernatural horror and eccentric companions. A new cast gives the series another starting point while retaining its timing-based battles. The journey becomes an investigation whose strange encounters matter both to the mystery and to the party gradually assembled around it.

cards.heading: A new cast crosses an unfamiliar America
cards.text: Shadow Hearts: From the New World is Nautilus's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 28 July 2005. Johnny Garland, an amnesiac private investigator, travels with Shania in pursuit of the dangerous Lady through an alternate Prohibition-era America. The setting combines recognisable places and history with supernatural horror and eccentric companions. A new cast gives the series another starting point while retaining its timing-based battles. The journey becomes an investigation whose strange encounters matter both to the mystery and to the party gradually assembled around it.

cards.heading: A command still needs the right timing
cards.text: The Judgement Ring asks the player to time an input within marked areas after selecting an action. Combat therefore adds a physical performance to the usual decision about which character should attack, heal or use a skill. A party of up to four characters brings different abilities into that system. Choosing an effective plan is only part of carrying it out; the player must still execute the ring input reliably. The repeated timing gives otherwise familiar role-playing battles another rhythm, keeping attention on each action instead of treating its selection as the end of the turn.

cards.heading: The final Shadow Hearts from Nautilus
cards.text: Takamusa Ohsawa directed and produced the game after working on Covenant, with Miyako Kato returning to design the characters. Yoshitaka Hirota led a score also credited to Tomoko Imoto and Ryo Fukuda. The North American release followed in 2006 and Europe in 2007. Development focused on refining the preceding game's mechanics while introducing a new setting and group. It became Nautilus's final game before the studio was absorbed into Aruze and left development, closing the original series with another mixture of historical travel, improbable personalities and carefully timed combat.

main.title: Pac 'n Roll
main.summary: Pac 'n Roll is a 2005 puzzle platformer video game developed and published by Namco for the Nintendo DS.

cards.text: Pac 'n Roll is a 2005 puzzle platformer video game developed and published by Namco for the Nintendo DS. The player is tasked with controlling Pac-Man through different levels, with its controls centered around using the touch screen. The harder the player swipes on the screen, the faster Pac-Man goes in the respective direction. In each level, the player must navigate Pac-Man from the beginning to the end while dodging different obstacles, such as ghosts, and collecting enough "pellets" to unlock the next area. The game also features boss fights and additional unlockable challenges on each stage.

The game was first showcased at E3 2004 as one of the first games showcased for the then-newly announced Nintendo DS. It was then formally announced in early 2005 and released throughout the latter part of that year, starting with July 28, 2005 in Japan. It received mixed reviews from critics, who were generally positive of the gameplay mechanics, but divided on its difficulty and depth, and generally criticized the story. It was later re-released as Pac 'n Roll Remix, a remake originally included as part of the Namco Museum Remix compilation for the Wii in 2007. Pac 'n Roll Remix was later included as part of Pac-Man Museum+, another video game compilation that was released for several platforms in 2022.

main.title: Grandia III
main.subtitle: A would-be pilot meets someone with another calling
main.summary: Grandia III is Game Arts' PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 4 August 2005. Yuki dreams of becoming a great pilot in a world where aircraft use magical power. Meeting Alfina, who can communicate with the world's Guardians, carries that ambition into a much larger journey. The player travels with a changing party through a story that connects flight, family and spiritual danger. The series' familiar interest in adventure is expressed through movement between places, while its battle system makes the timing of actions important within each encounter.

cards.heading: A would-be pilot meets someone with another calling
cards.text: Grandia III is Game Arts' PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 4 August 2005. Yuki dreams of becoming a great pilot in a world where aircraft use magical power. Meeting Alfina, who can communicate with the world's Guardians, carries that ambition into a much larger journey. The player travels with a changing party through a story that connects flight, family and spiritual danger. The series' familiar interest in adventure is expressed through movement between places, while its battle system makes the timing of actions important within each encounter.

cards.heading: Watch when the next action will arrive
cards.text: The combat timeline shows the approach of allied and enemy actions, allowing the player to judge which attack or technique can intervene at a useful moment. Position and timing turn a selected command into part of a larger sequence rather than an isolated exchange. Guardians offer further help as the campaign progresses. Between encounters, Yuki's aircraft replaces a conventional walking world map, with new landing points opening as the story advances. The player's expanding ability to travel therefore remains visible, connecting a young pilot's ambition to the practical structure of reaching the next part of the adventure.

cards.heading: A familiar battle tradition on PlayStation 2
cards.text: Hidenobu Takahashi directed the game, with returning series composer Noriyuki Iwadare supplying the score and Miz performing the opening song In the Sky. Much of the team had worked on earlier Grandia releases. North America received the game in February 2006, while Europe did not receive an original edition. Reviews were generally favourable, particularly towards the combat system. Grandia III carries forward the series' way of making battle timing readable, placing that carefully ordered rhythm beside a story whose protagonist is eager to rise above his starting point and discover a wider world.

main.title: Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness
main.subtitle: Genius Sonority · GameCube
main.summary: Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness is Genius Sonority's GameCube role-playing adventure returning to the region of Orre after Pokémon Colosseum. A new young trainer confronts Cipher's renewed use of Shadow Pokémon, with the imposing Shadow Lugia becoming the central image of the threat. The Snag Machine again allows the player to rescue affected creatures from opposing trainers. Double Battles carry the main journey, asking the developing party to respond to two enemies at once while preserving the opportunity to bring a Shadow Pokémon safely into the team.

cards.heading: Return to Orre and its Shadow Pokémon
cards.text: Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness is Genius Sonority's GameCube role-playing adventure returning to the region of Orre after Pokémon Colosseum. A new young trainer confronts Cipher's renewed use of Shadow Pokémon, with the imposing Shadow Lugia becoming the central image of the threat. The Snag Machine again allows the player to rescue affected creatures from opposing trainers. Double Battles carry the main journey, asking the developing party to respond to two enemies at once while preserving the opportunity to bring a Shadow Pokémon safely into the team.

cards.heading: Purification becomes a system to arrange
cards.text: Captured Shadow Pokémon need to be purified before they can fully return to ordinary life. Carrying one in the party remains useful, while the Purification Chamber lets the player arrange Pokémon into sets that support the process. The larger group therefore contributes beyond the six creatures currently travelling together. Shadow attacks create their own relationships in combat, and missed captures can receive another opportunity through returning rival Miror B. The rescue campaign connects the encounter in front of the player to the collection being cared for elsewhere.

cards.heading: More ways to meet a Pokémon
cards.text: Poké Spots introduce limited wild encounters after bait has attracted a creature, adding another route to expanding the collection. Battle SIMs and Battle Bingo provide challenges built around prepared teams or particular rules. The game also connects with the Game Boy Advance Pokémon titles for trading and battle. Released in 2005, XD developed the distinctive home-console approach established by Colosseum: a story-led journey whose Pokémon are encountered through another trainer's actions, then gradually restored through the player's attention after the fight has ended.

main.title: Geist
main.subtitle: A scientist separated from his body
main.summary: Geist is n-Space's action adventure, first released for GameCube in North America on 15 August 2005.

cards.heading: A scientist separated from his body
cards.text: Geist is n-Space's action adventure, first released for GameCube in North America on 15 August 2005. Scientist John Raimi is captured during an investigation and separated from his body. As a spirit, he searches the Volks Corporation's facilities for a way back. Possession connects its puzzles and first-person combat: the next useful ability belongs to something or someone Raimi must first find a way to inhabit.

cards.heading: Frighten a host to find a way forward
cards.text: Objects provide a means of affecting the physical world. Raimi can animate or alter them to frighten a person or animal, making that creature vulnerable to possession. A guard may supply a weapon and access to another room; a smaller animal may reach a narrow opening. Looking around therefore means considering potential hosts as well as doors and enemies.

cards.heading: Borrow another view of the world
cards.text: Leaving a host changes the pace and appearance of the surrounding world, but Raimi cannot remain unattached indefinitely. Another possession anchors him again and supplies a different set of abilities. The player repeatedly shifts between observing a situation as a ghost and acting through a borrowed body. That change of viewpoint gives an ordinary room several possible routes, depending on whose senses and movements are available.

main.title: Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow
main.subtitle: Soma's inheritance returns
main.summary: Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow is Konami's action role-playing adventure for Nintendo DS and a sequel to Aria of Sorrow. Soma Cruz is drawn back into danger by a cult seeking the return of a Dark Lord. Exploration unfolds across an interconnected castle, with equipment, experience and new abilities gradually expanding what Soma can reach. The side-on action retains the directness of a platform game, while its larger structure rewards returning to a familiar corridor with a power that changes the route through it.

cards.heading: Soma's inheritance returns
cards.text: Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow is Konami's action role-playing adventure for Nintendo DS and a sequel to Aria of Sorrow. Soma Cruz is drawn back into danger by a cult seeking the return of a Dark Lord. Exploration unfolds across an interconnected castle, with equipment, experience and new abilities gradually expanding what Soma can reach. The side-on action retains the directness of a platform game, while its larger structure rewards returning to a familiar corridor with a power that changes the route through it.

cards.heading: The abilities of an enemy
cards.text: The Tactical Soul system lets Soma acquire abilities from defeated creatures. An enemy is consequently more than an obstacle or a source of experience: it may provide a new attack or another useful effect. Equipment and soul choices allow the player to prepare for a particular fight, while the castle's passages encourage experimentation outside combat. A collection grows through ordinary exploration. The system gives repeated encounters an additional purpose, because the creature already recognised on screen can still have something valuable left to offer.

cards.heading: A final mark on the screen
cards.text: Dawn of Sorrow adds Magic Seals, patterns that must be traced with the stylus to finish important enemies. A boss encounter can therefore move from buttons to a brief drawing action at its conclusion. The second screen also makes information available while Soma continues exploring below. Konami combines these DS-specific gestures with the progression inherited from Aria of Sorrow. The central pleasure remains learning the castle and reshaping Soma's abilities, with the new hardware changing particular moments rather than the whole rhythm of the adventure.

main.title: Burnout Revenge
main.subtitle: Turning traffic into a weapon
main.summary: Speed is only the beginning. Burnout Revenge builds its races around traffic, close calls and deliberate collisions, making risk a resource that can carry a driver from a near miss into a spectacular takedown.

cards.heading: Checking traffic at racing speed
cards.text: Burnout Revenge is Criterion's racing game built around high speed, close calls and deliberate collisions. Its traffic-checking system lets the player hit many vehicles travelling in the same direction, sending them into rivals or other cars. Buses, heavy trucks and oncoming traffic remain dangerous. Reading the road means quickly distinguishing a useful target from an obstacle that will end the run. Traffic Attack builds an entire mode around this ability to knock cars off the road.

cards.heading: Finding the driver who took you down
cards.text: A driver who takes the player down can become a particular target for revenge. Criterion gave the returning attack extra importance, encouraging players to recognise and pursue the opponent responsible for their crash. This gives a crowded race a small personal history. Alongside finding a quick line and staying ahead, the player has another reason to watch a certain car and wait for an opportunity to strike.

cards.heading: Sharing the crash on Xbox 360
cards.text: The Xbox 360 edition, released in North America on March 7, 2006, added Live Revenge and Save & Share. Live Revenge records rivalries between online players and highlights their past results against one another. Save & Share lets players select moments from replays, save them and share them with others. A spectacular takedown can become a clip to show and rate after the race, extending the pleasure of a crash beyond the moment of impact.
